# Proof

**Conventions.** For a continuous $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ write $f=u+iv$ with $u=\operatorname{Re} f$, $v=\operatorname{Im} f$. Since $|u(s)-u(t)|\le|f(s)-f(t)|$ and $|v(s)-v(t)|\le|f(s)-f(t)|$, both $u,v:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous. The complex integral over $[p,q]\subseteq[a,b]$ is defined by
$$\int_p^q f(t)\,dt=\int_p^q u(t)\,dt+i\int_p^q v(t)\,dt,$$
where the right-hand integrals are (Riemann/Darboux) integrals of real functions; by convention $\int_p^p g=0$. Continuous real functions on a closed bounded interval are Riemann integrable, and the restriction of a continuous function to a closed subinterval is continuous, so all integrals below exist.

## Step 1: the real case

**Lemma.** Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and $c\in[a,b]$. Then $\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g=\int_a^b g$.

*Proof.* If $c=a$, then $\int_a^a g=0$ and the identity reads $\int_a^b g=\int_a^b g$. If $c=b$, likewise $\int_b^b g=0$. (If $a=b$ then $c=a=b$, covered.) So assume $a<c<b$.

For a partition $P$ of an interval $I$ let $L(g,P)$ and $U(g,P)$ be the lower and upper Darboux sums. Since $g$ is integrable on each of $[a,c]$, $[c,b]$, $[a,b]$, its integral there equals both the supremum of lower sums and the infimum of upper sums over partitions of that interval; in particular $L(g,P)\le\int_I g\le U(g,P)$ for every partition $P$ of $I$.

Let $P_1=\{a=x_0<\dots<x_m=c\}$ be any partition of $[a,c]$ and $P_2=\{c=y_0<\dots<y_n=b\}$ any partition of $[c,b]$. Then $P=P_1\cup P_2$ is a partition of $[a,b]$ whose subintervals are exactly those of $P_1$ together with those of $P_2$ (the point $c$ is shared; no subinterval straddles $c$). Since Darboux sums are sums over subintervals,
$$L(g,P)=L(g,P_1)+L(g,P_2),\qquad U(g,P)=U(g,P_1)+U(g,P_2).$$
Hence
$$L(g,P_1)+L(g,P_2)\le\int_a^b g\le U(g,P_1)+U(g,P_2).$$
Fix $P_2$ and take the supremum over $P_1$ in the left inequality: $\int_a^c g+L(g,P_2)\le\int_a^b g$; then take the supremum over $P_2$: $\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g\le\int_a^b g$. Similarly, taking infima over $P_1$ and then $P_2$ in the right inequality gives $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$. Therefore equality holds. $\square$

## Step 2: the complex case

Apply the Lemma to $u$ and to $v$ (both continuous on $[a,b]$):
$$\int_a^c u+\int_c^b u=\int_a^b u,\qquad \int_a^c v+\int_c^b v=\int_a^b v.$$
Then, by the definition of the complex integral and the rules of addition in $\mathbb C$,
$$\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f=\Big(\int_a^c u+i\int_a^c v\Big)+\Big(\int_c^b u+i\int_c^b v\Big)
=\Big(\int_a^c u+\int_c^b u\Big)+i\Big(\int_a^c v+\int_c^b v\Big)=\int_a^b u+i\int_a^b v=\int_a^b f.$$
This proves $\displaystyle\int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt$. $\blacksquare$
